statements.text: The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) intends to surpass us as the frontrunner in scientific knowledge and technological development, and they’re committing extensive resources to crucial technologies like artificial intelligence, quantum information sciences, critical mineral development and advanced manufacturing. Falling behind will threaten our national security, our global competitiveness, and jobs here at home.
statements.venue: Op-ed in The Oklahoman, co-authored with Rep. Frank Lucas

statements.text: We have seen AI in the legislative branch assist library patrons with optical character recognition, building LLM models to allow experimentation and tests based on high-quality Government data or reports, and work to upskill legislative branch staff to become familiar with generative AI technology. The first question I have, in the 2023 year-end report on the Federal judiciary, Chief Justice Roberts cautioned the judicial branch that, quote, ``Any use of AI requires caution and humility.'' I think we are here today in that spirit to acknowledge the first steps of the legislative branch must be cautious, humble, thoughtful and forward-looking.
statements.context: House committee hearing on AI innovations within the legislative branch, January 30, 2024.

statements.text: Large language models are being weaponized. In December, VentureBeat published an article about LLM attacks against members of the U.K. Parliament. In this instance, hackers used them to personalize emails and kept sending new emails in rapid succession until they got through.
statements.context: House hearing on AI innovations within the Legislative Branch, where Rep. Bice questions a witness about vendor vetting and LLM-enabled attacks.

statements.text: The second thing is, you mentioned AI, and I think that looking at whether or not we have the opportunity to utilize AI to create those bill summaries is really, I think, important. I also agree with you, that caution has to be had, though, because if we were participating or listened to the hearing yesterday, which was really about AI and the legislative process, there was a lot of conversation around inaccurate information being presented.
statements.context: House legislative hearing on modernizing the Congressional Research Service and federal data use.

statements.text: Last, I want to talk a little bit about AI and data governance, which is something I know that your office has been looking into. [...] Can you share a bit more about testing that should be taking place before the implementation of that technology?
statements.context: House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on the Office of the Clerk, discussing operational tools and AI governance for legislative support functions.

statements.text: We’ve got to do something, and we need to do it quickly. The challenge that you face is being restrictive enough that you’re making an impact but not being too restrictive that it impacts business, and there really is a fine line for that.
statements.venue: Journal Record, remarks to Greater Oklahoma City Chamber on regulating AI

statements.text: Bringing Microsoft Copilot to the House community is a great example of how the Subcommittee is leaning into this work. [...] Integrating AI technologies into House operations is a game-changing first step in making the House a more efficient and effective institution.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Administration Subcommittee on Modernization and Innovation hearing

statements.text: The demand is clearly there, and staff are not going to wait for the House, the Library, or CRS [Congressional Research Service] to build the tools they need
statements.venue: Opening remarks, subcommittee hearing on legislative data

statements.text: The House AI Innovators Pipeline will accelerate ongoing innovation and ensure Congress remains current in a rapidly changing world.
statements.venue: Press release on House AI Innovators Pipeline launch
